Why AppLovin’s Discount May Be Unwarranted Ahead of Q3
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 9:18 PM CDT 4 min read
AppLovin (NASDAQ:APP) reports third-quarter results in early November, and the question hanging over it is whether the company can keep growing this fast. In the second quarter, revenue rose 53% to $1,924 million, and net income grew even faster.
Yet the stock is priced as if that pace is about to fade. At about 16 times forward earnings, AppLovin sits far below the multiple it has averaged over the past five years. The facts support a view that the discount is wider than the business justifies, though one weakness keeps that view from being a strong one.
AppLovin sells advertising software that works for the advertiser. Its AI-powered platform, called AppLovin Ads, helps businesses decide where to place their ads, and the company's quarterly filing says substantially all of its revenue comes from it. That makes the platform both the engine of the story and its main risk. If you're interested in AI investing, we recently compiled a report on 10 Undervalued AI Stocks to Buy Now.
Over the past 12 months, AppLovin's operating margin was about 78%. In the second quarter, its adjusted EBITDA margin reached 84%. A margin that high usually means each added dollar of sales costs the company very little to earn, which is the clearest sign of an edge in the software itself.
Free cash flow backs that up at $863.3 million for the quarter, and management put part of it into buying back the company's own shares. Sales are also spread across regions: U.S. revenue was $989.6 million in the quarter, and the rest of the world brought in $934.1 million.
Revenue grew about 30% a year over the past five years, so the latest quarter came on top of a long record. The same quarter a year earlier brought in $1,259 million, far below this year's. For investors looking for profitable software names, our list of 10 Most Profitable Software Stocks to Buy Right Now is worth a look.
The fair objection is concentration, since the filing ties substantially all revenue to AppLovin Ads. It also names e-commerce as a new market the company hopes to win, which is a goal rather than a result so far.
Guidance also points to a small step down in margin, with management expecting an adjusted EBITDA margin of 83% in the third quarter, below the second quarter's level.
That margin move is too small to change the view. Concentration does cap it, because a stumble in one product has nothing to cushion it. A shareholder owns one very profitable engine, with the next one still unproven. Two things would settle the question: e-commerce turning from a stated goal into revenue the company reports, and margins holding near their current level as the platform grows. Investors who want more beaten-down names can see our ranking of 10 Stocks Investors Are Running Away From.
On adjusted earnings, the forward multiple of about 16 sits about 25% above its sector's median and about 45% below AppLovin's own five-year average. So the stock costs more than a typical company in its sector, but far less than investors have usually paid for it. On a stricter GAAP basis, the multiple would look somewhat higher.
That price assumes growth fades much faster than the latest quarter suggests. For a shareholder, it leaves room for some slowing before the numbers disappoint. If you're looking for cheaper growth names, check out 10 Undervalued Growth Stocks to Buy Now.
Early November's report will show whether last quarter's growth was a speed-up or a peak. AppLovin has earned the benefit of the doubt on profit, but it hasn't yet shown a second source of revenue. Revenue inside the guided range of $2,055 million to $2,085 million, with the margin near 83%, would make a deep discount to history harder to defend.
While we acknowledge the risk and potential of APP as an investment, our conviction lies in the belief that some AI stocks hold greater promise for delivering higher returns and doing so within a shorter time frame. AppLovin Falls 3% as Wells Fargo Calls Pixel Install Spike a False Start; Trade Desk Sits Out the Selloff, Magnite Dips
Wells Fargo just challenged the metric investors have been using to track AppLovin's e-commerce progress, and the stock is paying for it. Whether the firm's skepticism holds or gets overturned by better data could define where AppLovin heads from here.
Published October 1, 2026, 12:02pm ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
Business professionals analyze data with a digital overlay of advertising concepts, illustrating the dynamic landscape of online ad spending that companies like Meta Platforms are navigating. © Summit Art Creations / Shutterstock.com
A single research note is reopening the debate over how much real merchant traction sits behind AppLovin‘s (NASDAQ:APP | APP Price Prediction) e-commerce push. AppLovin stock is down 3% to $281.31 this morning. Meanwhile, shares of The Trade Desk (NASDAQ:TTD) are up 0.2% to $12.20, sitting out the selling that has hit AppLovin stock.
Magnite (NASDAQ:MGNI) shares are sliding 0.7% to $25.08, a far softer decline than the one in AppLovin stock. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) is also down 0.1% to $738.80, leaving large-cap technology close to flat. Taken together, those moves frame the drop in AppLovin stock as a repricing of one company’s growth story, with little evidence of a broad ad-tech selloff.
Wells Fargo Calls the Pixel Spike a False Start
The pressure traces to a note from Wells Fargo (NYSE:WFC) telling clients that a recent spike in merchant Pixel installs at AppLovin looks weaker than the raw count suggests. Investors asked about Pixel adds over the past two weeks. Wells Fargo found that raw installs did rise while the mix of new sites failed to improve. Most of the new sites, the firm determined, were Asia-Pacific storefronts built on Shopify (NASDAQ:SHOP) with little or no measurable web traffic.
On a traffic-weighted basis, Wells Fargo sees no meaningful pickup, pushing back on the idea that AppLovin’s e-commerce customer growth had suddenly accelerated. Calling the burst a false start, the firm stated that a real e-commerce turn at AppLovin still looks more like a story for next year. Wells Fargo kept an Equal Weight rating and a $325 price target on AppLovin stock.
Analysts treat new Pixel installs as a merchant testing count. The tally is one of the few public indicators for whether AppLovin’s web advertising push is landing real stores. That role explains why a note on install quality is weighing on AppLovin stock, where selling centers on a measurement question with Wells Fargo challenging what the install count means for AppLovin’s merchant growth.
In any case, AppLovin stock is down 58% year-to-date. That steep slide has made AppLovin shares highly sensitive to any read on the company’s web advertising push, and a single note on install quality was enough to add fresh pressure.
Notably, Trade Desk stock is barely changed and Magnite shares are only slightly lower, which points to an AppLovin-specific repricing.
Fresh Pixel data showing installs from storefronts with measurable traffic could answer the core objection in the Wells Fargo note on AppLovin. A traffic-weighted pickup would challenge the firm’s view that a real e-commerce turn at AppLovin belongs to next year. Any shift in the mix toward higher-traffic merchants could matter more for AppLovin than the raw install total.
Careful calibration of one’s holdings makes sense given AppLovin’s 58% decline year-to-date and a Wells Fargo timeline that places a real e-commerce turn next year. Patience may be the best attitude toward AppLovin stock while the market sorts out how much of the company’s web growth reflects real merchants.

pages.title: Mobile tracker claims, the Supercell deal that never happened, Mario Kart Tour's closure and AppLovin vs Unity | Week in Views  | PocketGamer.biz
pages.text:
Mobile tracker claims, the Supercell deal that never happened, Mario Kart Tour's closure and AppLovin vs Unity | Week in Views
The Pocketgamer.biz team pick their highlights from the headlines this week and deliver the stories behind the stories
Share:
The games industry moves quickly and while stories may come and go there are some that we just can't let go of…
So, to give those particularly thorny topics a further going over we've created a weekly digest where the members of the PocketGamer.biz team share their thoughts and go that little bit deeper on some of the more interesting things that have happened in mobile gaming in the past week.
Questioning that report on mobile games ‘infested’ with trackers and where your data gets sent
A questionable report released today by ProtonVPN carries with it bold claims that some of the biggest mobile games in the world are “infested” with trackers that send your data to China, Russia, Israel and ‘Five Eyes’.
I found the report a strange one, yet it's been reported by a couple media outlets as is so far.
FYI I'm sure you know, but Five Eyes is an intelligence-sharing alliance that consists of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, United Kingdom and United States.
The report says some of the “trackers” included in games can send “large amounts of highly personal data to countries hostile to privacy, with minimal transparency and no meaningful accountability”.
The report examined the 100 most downloaded mobile games in countries such as the US, UK and Germany. In the US, it found that of the (presumably estimated) downloads, 98% of them send data to ‘Five Eyes entities’(?), 95% to Israel, 81% to China, 71% to Russia and 70% to all of the countries it looked into.
So what does this actually mean in practice, though? The report used open-source platform Exodus Privacy to analyse Android apps and detect ad trackers.
This then details widely-used ad networks on mobile - some of them simply headquartered in the named countries. I looked at one top game to see exactly what kind of trackers the report alludes to.
These include AppLovin, AppsFlyer, Facebook Ads, Google AdMob, IronSource (wasn’t this shut down?), Tapjoy, Unity Ads and others. Hardly insidious.
These companies and networks, of course, are just par for the course on mobile and key networks for running ads and driving user acquisition campaigns.
The insinuation that simply from this, your personal - and identifiable - data is then shared with government agencies or is accessible by criminals for some nefarious purpose that will impact your life seems disingenuous.
Part of the report states how some apps actively collect users’ physical location - but takes no lengths to explain how this information is tracked to individual users by external parties or, importantly, that location sharing permissions are strictly opt-in for Google Play.
It’s worth noting that the report also includes a link trying to sell the company's ad blocker included in paid plans.
I think there are some practices that could shock people (like panel data), but just reeling off ad companies and stoking up political tensions is, as I’ve said, in my opinion disingenuous.
I asked ProtonVPN for comment and they sent the following statement:
“This report is about exposure of data, not about proven misuse. We're not claiming that any specific government has accessed data from these games, but we're showing that the most popular games in the world contain trackers that send data to companies with links to countries such as China and Russia. In China, for instance, National Intelligence Law requires organisations to support state intelligence work. In Russia, surveillance rules give security services broad access to data held by Russian companies.
“Some apps may have a valid reason for collecting location information, but when this is tied to extensive data sharing (e.g. the apps with large numbers of trackers), then there is the question of what else may be done with the data. Most naturally, this would most naturally be used to enhance the performance of ad targeting by sharing it with international ad networks (some of which are in locations that a user may not be comfortable with).
“Some apps are quite meticulous with specifying in their privacy policies which ad networks and external analytics providers that they are sharing data with. Others make broader, non-specific statements. And some have privacy policies that make no reference to the trackers that they have, and seem more like generic website privacy policies taken from a template library to satisfy the requirements of having a policy. Of course, few people take the time to read privacy policies, as well.”
Mark Pincus reveals Zynga nearly acquired Supercell for $400m in 2012
There’s something interesting about the “what if?” stories that occasionally come out of the games industry. We hear about acquisitions that never happened, or job moves that could have gone a different way. Countless huge deals must have come close to happening, then fell apart, and we’ll probably never know about them.
This is a particularly interesting one, with Zynga’s founder Mark Pincus claiming he had a handshake agreement with Supercell CEO Ilkka Paananen to acquire the developer for $400 million in 2012, only for Zynga’s board to reject the deal.
You can understand why. Zynga had already had a rough experience with the acquisition of OMGPOP, which had made a popular title with Draw Something. However, the game’s popularity quickly faded. The board apparently didn’t want Pincus making another acquisition before proving he could manage what he already had.
But the timing makes this one pretty painful in hindsight. Pincus says Zynga was already watching Supercell closely, with Hay Day and Clash of Clans taking off. Supercell would, of course, go on to become one of the biggest success stories in mobile games.
It does make you wonder how many other massive deals have come this close and never happened.
Mario Kart Tour shuts down after seven years on mobile
This is a strange one for me. Despite being a big Nintendo fan, I never actually played Mario Kart Tour, so I can’t claim its closure affects me personally. And yet, I have a very clear sense of nostalgia for this mobile racing game.
I had just started university when Mario Kart Tour released, and I vividly remember my first time seeing the game in-person was on a new housemate’s phone as I walked into the kitchen. It sparked a conversation, I watched some gameplay, shared some information from the handful of videos I’d seen from Nintendo YouTubers, and suddenly that new housemate was that little bit easier to talk to.
I saw a few people playing it around that time - not big Nintendo fans, not Switch owners, but young adults who were nostalgic for Mario Kart Wii and gave the game a try. As for how many stuck with it for the duration, who’s to know. But for those who did, it seems a shame there’s no Complete Edition like Animal Crossing: Pocket Camp got when that game shut down. It’s a reminder that most live service games will only live for so long.
AppLovin takes legal action against Unity over Ad Quality DSP
This week, Paige covered the news that AppLovin is taking legal action against Unity over data collected through the latter’s Ad Quality SDK.
If you've been following mobile ad tech, AppLovin and Unity ending up in court probably doesn't come as a huge shock.
According to the lawsuit, AppLovin asked a San Francisco court to stop Unity from collecting data through its Ad Quality tool. AppLovin says the tool picks up information about the ads AppLovin wins and that Unity might be using that data to train models that bid against it. Unity says the data comes from developers who agreed to share it and calls the lawsuit a dominant company trying to handle competition through the courts.
In mobile ads, data is the product, so I can see why AppLovin is worried. But suing a rival as competition heats up isn't a great look either. It's also hard to ignore the history here - not long ago, AppLovin tried to buy Unity outright.
What I keep coming back to when I think about this case is the developers in the middle. It's their games and their players, yet the fight over that data is happening without them.
Nothing's been decided yet, but I'm curious to see where this one lands!

Unity Software Sinks 10% Despite Wedbush Target Hike on Vector Ad Platform; AppLovin Falls 3%, Trade Desk Slips
Wedbush just raised its price target on Unity Software and praised its Vector ad platform, yet the stock is sinking hard while rivals escape with minor bruises. Something beyond the numbers is spooking investors, and the answer cuts to the…
Published October 14, 2026, 1:57pm ET · 3 min read
Market Movers desk. Editor: David Moadel.
An investor reacts to a plummeting stock chart, reflecting the market's descent into 'Extreme Fear' as key tech stocks sink. © Atichat Wattanasin Stone / Shutterstock.com
Unity Software (NYSE:U | U Price Prediction) stock is trading at $42.13, down 10% this afternoon. Wedbush raised its price target on Unity shares and described the company’s Vector advertising platform as gaining traction. That decline suggests the advertising cycle is weighing more heavily than the platform’s progress.
Meanwhile, AppLovin (NASDAQ:APP) stock is at $263.65, down 3%, a softer pullback than the one in Unity Software stock. Additionally, shares of The Trade Desk (NASDAQ:TTD) are at $11.94, down 2%, a smaller slide than AppLovin’s. Those declines confirm pressure across ad-tech, with Unity Software stock at the heavy end.
For sector-level and broad-market gauges, the Fidelity MSCI Communication Services Index ETF (NYSEARCA:FCOM) is down 2%, and the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is down 1%. Thus, the drop in Unity Software stock stands out. This is notable against that background, since it’s several times the size of the move across the rest of the digital advertising group.
Strong numbers back the price target raise. In Q2 2026, Unity Software’s revenue rose 23.9% year over year to $546.47 million, topping expectations. Its adjusted earnings per share (EPS) of $0.28 also beat estimates.
Grow Solutions, the segment that houses Vector inside the Unity Ads Network, expanded 35% to $389 million. Unity Software’s Q3 2026 outlook calls for strategic revenue of $540 million to $550 million. The company is targeting generally accepted accounting principles (GAAP) profitability as soon as that quarter. Yet, Unity Software shares are sliding anyway, as cyclical ad-spending worries outweigh execution.
Unity Software runs two businesses: the game engine studios build on, and an advertising network that places and monetizes ads inside mobile games. Vector lives in the ad network, competing with AppLovin for advertising spend. Create Solutions, the engine side, grew just 2% in the second quarter, leaving most of the growth burden on Vector.
AppLovin brings far greater scale, with second-quarter revenue up 52.8% year over year to $1.92 billion. Year to date (YTD), AppLovin stock was down 61%, a much steeper slide than the 5% decline in Unity Software stock.
The Trade Desk operates as a demand-side bidding platform. So its business tracks broad advertising budgets across connected TV, mobile, display and other formats. Its second-quarter revenue rose just 3% year over year to $715.1 million, missing expectations. Down 69% YTD, Trade Desk stock now trades at a P/E ratio of 12x.
FCOM holds no AppLovin shares, making the Fidelity fund a broad gauge of advertising demand; its 2% decline doesn’t confirm selling in any single stock here. Trade Desk stock is a small position, at 0.5% of net assets.
The next test for Unity Software is whether Vector converts analyst enthusiasm into reported advertising revenue. A GAAP profit in the third quarter and the planned November payoff of the 2021 convertible notes would give the bull case steadier ground.
Unity has $2.36 billion in cash and an adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA) margin that expanded to 29% from 21% a year earlier. Its third-quarter guidance calls for adjusted EBITDA of $185 million to $190 million, pointing to further margin gains.
For Unity stock, the open question is whether Grow Solutions keeps expanding fast enough to back the bullish case. Keeping their positions smaller can help investors manage their risk until Vector’s revenue contribution is visible.

AppLovin Corporation (APP) Securities Class Action:
AppLovin provides end-to-end AI-powered advertising solutions for businesses to reach, monetize, and grow their global audience.
To investors, "uplift" is possibly the most critical driver of the company's revenue growth. The company improves its AI model to increase uplift, better matching the exact right ad to the exact right user at the exact right millisecond. In turn, this uplifts advertisers' return on ad spend, increases their advertising budgets, and (for AppLovin) accelerates high-margin revenue.
The lawsuit is focused on the propriety of AppLovin's statements about model improvements and uplift.
Most recently, several weeks into AppLovin's Q2, during its May 6, 2026 Q1 2026 earnings call, management left investors with high expectations for uplift and revenue growth.
CEO Adam Foroughi said that the most important milestone investors should focus on was the company's "improving the underlying model." He emphasized that "[l]ast quarter earnings, I mentioned we just had one new model that had just created an uplift[]" and "[t]he one we had a couple of weeks ago was quite substantial." He also explained, "that's why I highlighted […] that we saw a big acceleration going exiting the quarter[,]" and "then, April Q2, bigger than any quarter that we had[.]"
Investors' expectations began to unravel on July 13, 2026, when a prominent analyst published a report highlighting a lack of immediate advertiser influx following the general availability launch of AppLovin's advertising tools. In response, the price of AppLovin shares tumbled $64.13 (-12.6%).
Then, on August 5, 2026, the company reported its Q2 2026 revenue that was below midpoint. In apparent contrast to the "big acceleration," management said "[o]ur pace of meaningful model improvement was lighter than normal during the quarter[]" and "we didn't get the same level of model uplift we've seen in recent quarters[.]" This news drove the price of AppLovin shares crashing another $82.13 (-19.6%).
Between the two drops, the company lost over $44 billion of its market capitalization.
"We're focused on when during Q2 AppLovin first knew that the uplift and revenue acceleration investors had come to expect wasn't happening," said Reed Kathrein, the Hagens Berman partner leading the firm's investigation.

AppLovin Corporation (APP) Grew Revenue 53%. What Must Happen to Defend Its Valuation?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 10:32 AM CDT 5 min read
AppLovin Corporation (NASDAQ:APP) reported second-quarter 2026 revenue growth of 53%, yet its stock fell sharply after missing revenue expectations and management's own execution standard. The tension is not whether the advertising platform is growing; it is whether machine-learning improvements can sustain the exceptional margins and earnings trajectory implied by its valuation. In early October, analysts began questioning competing ad platforms' progress and the reliability of new e-commerce adoption signals. This makes AppLovin's stock less a straightforward growth story than a test of how durable its targeting advantage really is.
Second-quarter revenue reached $1.92 billion against a $1.94 billion consensus estimate, while EPS of $3.76 matched expectations. Adjusted EBITDA increased 58% to $1.61 billion, implying an adjusted EBITDA margin above 80%. Management said its important advertising-model upgrade arrived just after the quarter closed. The problem was timing rather than a reported collapse in customer demand, according to management, but the distinction matters only if later results confirm it.
AppLovin Corporation (NASDAQ:APP) ranks fourth among the 10 best undervalued stocks to buy now according to Reddit, behind three companies with very different economics. The more interesting comparison is whether AppLovin's extraordinary operating profitability can survive a market in which rivals increasingly adopt similar AI tools.
Zeta Global (ZETA) Tumbles as AI Dreams Turn to Nightmares
Incremental Compute Spending Could Help or Hurt
The company's advertising auctions improve as its models become more effective at predicting which ads produce sales. When advertisers earn better returns, they may expand budgets, giving AppLovin Corporation (NASDAQ:APP) more data and incremental revenue. The company guided Q3 revenue to $2.055 billion to $2.085 billion, up 46% to 48% year-over-year, alongside $1.71 billion to $1.74 billion of adjusted EBITDA and an approximately 83% margin. That guidance assumes model improvements already deployed, not hypothetical later releases.
Yet compute is not free. Management explained that higher training costs are being undertaken where incremental returns justify them. It said roughly ten cents of each incremental revenue dollar could be spent on compute. An 80%-plus adjusted EBITDA margin gives the company considerable room for investment, but also means small efficiency setbacks can have an outsized impact on investor assumptions about its operating leverage.
The expansion beyond games has its own measurement problem; how AppLovin is extending its AI platform into e-commerce advertising analyzes why a larger addressable market does not immediately translate into verified revenue. Competition is another pressure point. In October, a court declined AppLovin's request for interim relief concerning Unity's Ad Quality SDK, without ruling on the underlying allegations. Jefferies' survey of mobile-game ad buyers led it to raise estimates for Unity while lowering its 2027 AppLovin revenue forecast by 5% and EBITDA estimate by 7%.
The Discount Is Real, but So Is the Premium
The Seeking Alpha data places AppLovin Corporation (NASDAQ:APP) at 20.16 times trailing GAAP earnings and 16.76 times forward GAAP earnings, with forward non-GAAP P/E of 15.81. That last measure sits roughly 46% below the company's five-year average of 29.17, but about 26% above the sector median of 12.52. Forward enterprise value to sales is 10.91, nearly six times the sector median of 1.88. Accordingly, a much lower earnings multiple relative to AppLovin's history does not mean the business is inexpensive on every basis.
The consensus expects EPS growth of 60.49% in 2026, 27.30% in 2027, and 24.88% in 2028. The estimated P/E correspondingly falls from 16.76 on 2026 earnings to 13.16 on 2027 earnings and 10.54 on 2028 earnings, assuming a constant stock price and forecast delivery. The steepest growth is front-loaded, so valuation depends heavily on the bridge from rapid model-led gains to a more sustainable rate.
Free cash flow reached $863 million in Q2. Management expects full-year free cash flow conversion to normalize near 75% of adjusted EBITDA after tax and interest timing effects. The company ended the period with $3.05 billion in cash and around $3.7 billion in debt and repurchased or withheld about $551 million of stock. These are meaningful financial supports, but do not settle the question of how much customer acquisition efficiency can improve from today's elevated level.
Institutional Conviction Faces a Near-Term Test
Q2 2026 hedge fund ownership declined to 88 from 91 funds, while short positions increased to 11.61 million shares on September 30 from 10.56 million a month earlier, equaling 3.99% of float. The positioning is not exceptionally bearish by itself, but the direction contrasts with continued strong revenue growth.
Price-target cuts further illustrate the gap between current profitability and confidence in its future trajectory. On October 12, Oppenheimer reduced its target to $490 from $560 while lowering its FY2027 revenue and adjusted EBITDA forecasts; BofA maintained Neutral but reduced its target to $325 from $400 on October 9, arguing that a durable reacceleration would be needed to justify a premium to other advertising giants. Wedbush remained Outperform at $560 from $610 on October 14 but reset estimates to a more achievable baseline.
The immediate test is therefore not simply another 50% revenue-growth quarter. It is whether the Q3 model upgrade drives measurable ad spending, consumer-advertising diversification, and cash conversion without permanently higher compute intensity. A different Reddit screen asks which stocks investors expect to rise dramatically despite substantial uncertainty, underscoring the distinction between an exciting growth narrative and the earnings needed to support its price.

AppLovin (APP:NASDAQ) stock fell 12.6% in the month through October 19, compared with a 0.6% gain for the S&P 500.
Concerns about AI-model improvements, litigation, and analyst target reductions have weighed on sentiment.
Yet earnings expectations have held up considerably better than the stock price, raising an important question: Has the market already priced in too much bad news?
What's Driving AppLovin Stock Lower?
AppLovin reported second-quarter revenue of $1.924 billion, up 53% year over year but slightly below analysts' expectations of $1.94 billion.
CEO Adam Foroughi acknowledged weaker-than-usual improvements in the company's AI-driven advertising models during the quarter.
Meanwhile, AppLovin faced securities class-action allegations involving its AI technology and an ongoing legal dispute with Unity Software (U:NYSE).
For comparison, Unity reported second-quarter revenue of $546 million, up 24% year over year. AppLovin's 53% revenue growth was considerably faster, although the companies' business mixes differ.
That growth advantage matters, but investors are increasingly concerned about whether AppLovin can sustain its momentum.
Wall Street Is Cutting AppLovin's Price Targets
Seven major investment firms reduced their AppLovin price targets between October 8 and October 19.
Jefferies lowered its target from $550 to $375, while Citi reduced its target from $600 to $500.

However, a lower multiple does not automatically mean a stock is undervalued, particularly if future earnings expectations decline.
Is AppLovin Stock a Buy or Sell After Its 12% Drop?
AppLovin looks more like a cautious buying opportunity than a stock investors need to sell simply because of its recent decline.
The company continues to generate strong revenue growth, while its valuation has contracted significantly.
AppLovin expects third-quarter revenue between $2.055 billion and $2.085 billion, with adjusted EBITDA guidance of $1.710 billion to $1.740 billion.
AppLovin will report third-quarter results on November 4, after the market closes.
If AppLovin meets guidance and demonstrates renewed AI-model improvements, its discounted valuation could offer substantial long-term upside.
However, another disappointing quarter could trigger further earnings-estimate reductions and share-price pressure.
For patient investors, APP presents a potential buying opportunity rather than an obvious sell, but the November earnings report will be critical in determining whether the selloff has gone too far.

Questioning that report on mobile games ‘infested’ with trackers and where your data gets sent
A questionable report released today by ProtonVPN carries with it bold claims that some of the biggest mobile games in the world are “infested” with trackers that send your data to China, Russia, Israel and ‘Five Eyes’.
I found the report a strange one, yet it's been reported by a couple media outlets as is so far.
FYI I'm sure you know, but Five Eyes is an intelligence-sharing alliance that consists of Australia, Canada, New Zealand, United Kingdom and United States.
The report says some of the “trackers” included in games can send “large amounts of highly personal data to countries hostile to privacy, with minimal transparency and no meaningful accountability”.
The report examined the 100 most downloaded mobile games in countries such as the US, UK and Germany. In the US, it found that of the (presumably estimated) downloads, 98% of them send data to ‘Five Eyes entities’(?), 95% to Israel, 81% to China, 71% to Russia and 70% to all of the countries it looked into.
So what does this actually mean in practice, though? The report used open-source platform Exodus Privacy to analyse Android apps and detect ad trackers.
This then details widely-used ad networks on mobile - some of them simply headquartered in the named countries. I looked at one top game to see exactly what kind of trackers the report alludes to.
These include AppLovin, AppsFlyer, Facebook Ads, Google AdMob, IronSource (wasn’t this shut down?), Tapjoy, Unity Ads and others. Hardly insidious.
These companies and networks, of course, are just par for the course on mobile and key networks for running ads and driving user acquisition campaigns.
The insinuation that simply from this, your personal - and identifiable - data is then shared with government agencies or is accessible by criminals for some nefarious purpose that will impact your life seems disingenuous.
Part of the report states how some apps actively collect users’ physical location - but takes no lengths to explain how this information is tracked to individual users by external parties or, importantly, that location sharing permissions are strictly opt-in for Google Play.
It’s worth noting that the report also includes a link trying to sell the company's ad blocker included in paid plans.
I think there are some practices that could shock people (like panel data), but just reeling off ad companies and stoking up political tensions is, as I’ve said, in my opinion disingenuous.
I asked ProtonVPN for comment and they sent the following statement:
“This report is about exposure of data, not about proven misuse. We're not claiming that any specific government has accessed data from these games, but we're showing that the most popular games in the world contain trackers that send data to companies with links to countries such as China and Russia. In China, for instance, National Intelligence Law requires organisations to support state intelligence work. In Russia, surveillance rules give security services broad access to data held by Russian companies.
“Some apps may have a valid reason for collecting location information, but when this is tied to extensive data sharing (e.g. the apps with large numbers of trackers), then there is the question of what else may be done with the data. Most naturally, this would most naturally be used to enhance the performance of ad targeting by sharing it with international ad networks (some of which are in locations that a user may not be comfortable with).
“Some apps are quite meticulous with specifying in their privacy policies which ad networks and external analytics providers that they are sharing data with. Others make broader, non-specific statements. And some have privacy policies that make no reference to the trackers that they have, and seem more like generic website privacy policies taken from a template library to satisfy the requirements of having a policy. Of course, few people take the time to read privacy policies, as well.”
Mark Pincus reveals Zynga nearly acquired Supercell for $400m in 2012
There’s something interesting about the “what if?” stories that occasionally come out of the games industry. We hear about acquisitions that never happened, or job moves that could have gone a different way. Countless huge deals must have come close to happening, then fell apart, and we’ll probably never know about them.
This is a particularly interesting one, with Zynga’s founder Mark Pincus claiming he had a handshake agreement with Supercell CEO Ilkka Paananen to acquire the developer for $400 million in 2012, only for Zynga’s board to reject the deal.
You can understand why. Zynga had already had a rough experience with the acquisition of OMGPOP, which had made a popular title with Draw Something. However, the game’s popularity quickly faded. The board apparently didn’t want Pincus making another acquisition before proving he could manage what he already had.
But the timing makes this one pretty painful in hindsight. Pincus says Zynga was already watching Supercell closely, with Hay Day and Clash of Clans taking off. Supercell would, of course, go on to become one of the biggest success stories in mobile games.
It does make you wonder how many other massive deals have come this close and never happened.
Mario Kart Tour shuts down after seven years on mobile
This is a strange one for me. Despite being a big Nintendo fan, I never actually played Mario Kart Tour, so I can’t claim its closure affects me personally. And yet, I have a very clear sense of nostalgia for this mobile racing game.
I had just started university when Mario Kart Tour released, and I vividly remember my first time seeing the game in-person was on a new housemate’s phone as I walked into the kitchen. It sparked a conversation, I watched some gameplay, shared some information from the handful of videos I’d seen from Nintendo YouTubers, and suddenly that new housemate was that little bit easier to talk to.
I saw a few people playing it around that time - not big Nintendo fans, not Switch owners, but young adults who were nostalgic for Mario Kart Wii and gave the game a try. As for how many stuck with it for the duration, who’s to know. But for those who did, it seems a shame there’s no Complete Edition like Animal Crossing: Pocket Camp got when that game shut down. It’s a reminder that most live service games will only live for so long.
AppLovin takes legal action against Unity over Ad Quality DSP

In mobile ads, data is the product, so I can see why AppLovin is worried. But suing a rival as competition heats up isn't a great look either. It's also hard to ignore the history here - not long ago, AppLovin tried to buy Unity outright.
What I keep coming back to when I think about this case is the developers in the middle. It's their games and their players, yet the fight over that data is happening without them.
Nothing's been decided yet, but I'm curious to see where this one lands!

AppLovin Corporation (APP) Grew Revenue 53%. What Must Happen to Defend Its Valuation?
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 10:32 AM CDT 5 min read
AppLovin Corporation (NASDAQ:APP) reported second-quarter 2026 revenue growth of 53%, yet its stock fell sharply after missing revenue expectations and management's own execution standard. The tension is not whether the advertising platform is growing; it is whether machine-learning improvements can sustain the exceptional margins and earnings trajectory implied by its valuation. In early October, analysts began questioning competing ad platforms' progress and the reliability of new e-commerce adoption signals. This makes AppLovin's stock less a straightforward growth story than a test of how durable its targeting advantage really is.
Second-quarter revenue reached $1.92 billion against a $1.94 billion consensus estimate, while EPS of $3.76 matched expectations. Adjusted EBITDA increased 58% to $1.61 billion, implying an adjusted EBITDA margin above 80%. Management said its important advertising-model upgrade arrived just after the quarter closed. The problem was timing rather than a reported collapse in customer demand, according to management, but the distinction matters only if later results confirm it.
AppLovin Corporation (NASDAQ:APP) ranks fourth among the 10 best undervalued stocks to buy now according to Reddit, behind three companies with very different economics. The more interesting comparison is whether AppLovin's extraordinary operating profitability can survive a market in which rivals increasingly adopt similar AI tools.

Incremental Compute Spending Could Help or Hurt
The company's advertising auctions improve as its models become more effective at predicting which ads produce sales. When advertisers earn better returns, they may expand budgets, giving AppLovin Corporation (NASDAQ:APP) more data and incremental revenue. The company guided Q3 revenue to $2.055 billion to $2.085 billion, up 46% to 48% year-over-year, alongside $1.71 billion to $1.74 billion of adjusted EBITDA and an approximately 83% margin. That guidance assumes model improvements already deployed, not hypothetical later releases.
Yet compute is not free. Management explained that higher training costs are being undertaken where incremental returns justify them. It said roughly ten cents of each incremental revenue dollar could be spent on compute. An 80%-plus adjusted EBITDA margin gives the company considerable room for investment, but also means small efficiency setbacks can have an outsized impact on investor assumptions about its operating leverage.
The expansion beyond games has its own measurement problem; how AppLovin is extending its AI platform into e-commerce advertising analyzes why a larger addressable market does not immediately translate into verified revenue. Competition is another pressure point. In October, a court declined AppLovin's request for interim relief concerning Unity's Ad Quality SDK, without ruling on the underlying allegations. Jefferies' survey of mobile-game ad buyers led it to raise estimates for Unity while lowering its 2027 AppLovin revenue forecast by 5% and EBITDA estimate by 7%.
The Discount Is Real, but So Is the Premium
The Seeking Alpha data places AppLovin Corporation (NASDAQ:APP) at 20.16 times trailing GAAP earnings and 16.76 times forward GAAP earnings, with forward non-GAAP P/E of 15.81. That last measure sits roughly 46% below the company's five-year average of 29.17, but about 26% above the sector median of 12.52. Forward enterprise value to sales is 10.91, nearly six times the sector median of 1.88. Accordingly, a much lower earnings multiple relative to AppLovin's history does not mean the business is inexpensive on every basis.
The consensus expects EPS growth of 60.49% in 2026, 27.30% in 2027, and 24.88% in 2028. The estimated P/E correspondingly falls from 16.76 on 2026 earnings to 13.16 on 2027 earnings and 10.54 on 2028 earnings, assuming a constant stock price and forecast delivery. The steepest growth is front-loaded, so valuation depends heavily on the bridge from rapid model-led gains to a more sustainable rate.
Free cash flow reached $863 million in Q2. Management expects full-year free cash flow conversion to normalize near 75% of adjusted EBITDA after tax and interest timing effects. The company ended the period with $3.05 billion in cash and around $3.7 billion in debt and repurchased or withheld about $551 million of stock. These are meaningful financial supports, but do not settle the question of how much customer acquisition efficiency can improve from today's elevated level.
Institutional Conviction Faces a Near-Term Test
Q2 2026 hedge fund ownership declined to 88 from 91 funds, while short positions increased to 11.61 million shares on September 30 from 10.56 million a month earlier, equaling 3.99% of float. The positioning is not exceptionally bearish by itself, but the direction contrasts with continued strong revenue growth.
Price-target cuts further illustrate the gap between current profitability and confidence in its future trajectory. On October 12, Oppenheimer reduced its target to $490 from $560 while lowering its FY2027 revenue and adjusted EBITDA forecasts; BofA maintained Neutral but reduced its target to $325 from $400 on October 9, arguing that a durable reacceleration would be needed to justify a premium to other advertising giants. Wedbush remained Outperform at $560 from $610 on October 14 but reset estimates to a more achievable baseline.
The immediate test is therefore not simply another 50% revenue-growth quarter. It is whether the Q3 model upgrade drives measurable ad spending, consumer-advertising diversification, and cash conversion without permanently higher compute intensity.
